## MCP Console {#interactive-work .deck-slide .hero .story-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Why Console exists

:::

::: {.big-statement}

R, Python, and SQL.<br>One execution system.

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Shared state, session controls, and configurable permissions.

:::

::: {.notes}

MCP Console makes R, Python, and SQL available through one tool, with state that persists between calls. The model can use different languages for different parts of an analysis and move data between them.

The shared foundation handles session state, input, output, plots, package preparation, interrupts, and process cleanup. The application supplies the conversation; Console supplies the execution environment and applies the configured permissions.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Equip the model with R, Python, and SQL {#small-surface .deck-slide .story-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Languages available to the model

:::

:::: {.three-col}

::: {.story-card}

**R**

Statistical methods, analysis packages, and data visualization.

:::

::: {.story-card}

**Python**

Machine learning libraries and the broader Python ecosystem.

:::

::: {.story-card}

**SQL**

Local or remote database connections. Optimized queries.

:::

::::
::: {.takeaway}

The model can choose the language and syntax it works best with.

:::

::: {.notes}

The model can use R for its statistical methods and plotting tools, Python for its libraries, and SQL to query data. It can switch languages as the work develops, with the user steering that choice when needed.

R and Python can exchange objects in the same session. SQL can query R data frames through the managed DuckDB connection or use a connection selected by the user. Filesystem and network permissions apply around the runtime.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Full runtimes with explicit permissions {#sandbox-motivation .deck-slide .story-slide .capabilities-safety}
::: {.kicker}

A shared foundation for R, Python, and SQL

:::

:::: {.three-col}

::: {.story-card}

**Use full runtimes**

Libraries and native code.<br>Subprocesses and forks.<br>Text and plots.

:::

::: {.story-card}

**Drive a real session**

Persistent objects.<br>Input, waits, and controls.<br>Explicit runtime state.

:::

::: {.story-card}

**Enforce permissions**

Filesystem and network policy.<br>Subprocesses covered.<br>Shutdown and cleanup.

:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}

Persistent state, input, output, and controls across languages.

:::

::: {.notes}

Console runs the language runtimes with access to libraries, native code, and subprocesses under the user's configured permissions. It handles the session details around them: long computations, input prompts, interrupts, background output, plots, and large responses.

The embedded runtimes report when evaluation starts, waits for managed input, and finishes. Those state changes use explicit messages; ordinary output is collected separately. Native code can also read input or start background work that the runtime cannot fully observe.

The sandbox applies filesystem and network policy to the worker and its subprocesses. Package preparation uses separate trusted processes outside that sandbox. Sensitive files may need explicit read denials, and enforcement and cleanup have platform-specific limits. These boundaries are covered in the later examples.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md) · [Worker protocol](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/WORKER_PROTOCOL.md) · [Sandbox configuration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Send a cell of code {#send-r .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · one simple call

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

LLM client → Console

:::

<!-- cells:fit -->
```python
console.send(r="""
  d <- read.csv("examples/measurements.csv")
  fit <- lm(response ~ temperature + group,
            data = d)
  fit
""")
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R output

:::

```{r}
#| label: fit-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_text("fit")
```

::::

:::::

::::::
::: {.takeaway}

Define objects, see printed output, and continue in the same session.

:::

::: {.notes}

The basic operation is a call to `send` with a string of code. This R cell creates the data frame `d`, fits a linear model, and prints the fitted object. Both objects remain available for later calls.

The default slide render evaluates this example through knitr. The captured-output render uses the saved Console response.

[runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md) · [send](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md)

:::

## R and Python share the same process {#python-first .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · shared objects

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}
:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Python reads the R data frame

:::

<!-- reveal-cell:python-read-r -->
```python
console.send(python='len(r.d)')
```

::::
:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Console response

:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("language-reveal/python-read-r")
```

::::
:::::
::::: {.right}
:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

R reads the Python list

:::

<!-- reveal-cell:r-read-python -->
```python
console.send(r='length(py$values)')
```

::::
:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Console response

:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("language-reveal/r-read-python")
```

::::
:::::
::::::

::: {.takeaway}

`r.d` exposes the R object to Python. `py$values` exposes the Python object to R.

:::

::: {.notes}

R and Python are embedded in the same process, with reticulate providing the bridge. On the left, Python accesses `d` from R's global environment. On the right, R accesses `values` from Python's main dictionary.

This lets the model work with the same data across languages. Conversion depends on the object type; sharing a process does not mean every object is shared by reference or transferred without copying.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Query the same data with SQL {#sql .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · SQL in the same session

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

SQL cell

:::

<!-- cells:sql -->
```python
console.send(sql="""
SELECT "group", COUNT(*) AS n
FROM d
GROUP BY "group"
ORDER BY "group"
""")
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Captured result

:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("sql")
```

::::

:::::

::::::

::: {.notes}

The `sql` argument submits a query through the same tool. Here, `d` is the data frame created in R, rather than a table exported to a separate database.

The R-backed managed DuckDB connection finds data frames in R's global environment. Later queries see updated bindings if those objects are replaced. For this backend, Python data frames first need to be bound or converted to an R global.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## SQL uses the connection you choose {#sql-connections .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · choose the database connection

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R · a DBI connection

:::

```python
console.send(r="""
  con <- DBI::dbConnect(
    RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
  console_sql_connection(con)
""")
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Python · a DB-API connection

:::

```python
console.send(python="""
import sqlite3
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
console_sql_connection(con)
""")
```

::::

:::::

::::::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Subsequent SQL cells use the selected connection

:::

```python
console.send(sql="SELECT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP AS now")
```

::::

::: {.takeaway}

Use a local database or an existing remote connection through its driver.

:::

::: {.notes}

SQL can use a connection selected from either runtime: a DBI connection in R or a DB-API connection in Python. These examples use SQLite. A remote database needs its driver, credentials, and network access.

After selection, SQL cells use that connection's tables and state. They do not inherit the managed DuckDB registrations. Before closing a custom connection, restore managed SQL with `console_sql_connection(NULL)` in R or `console_sql_connection(None)` in Python.

[SQL connection selection](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md#sql)

:::
## Make CRAN and PyPI available to the session {#package-opportunity .deck-slide .story-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · packages

:::

::: {.story-lead}

A model may avoid a useful package to avoid changing the user’s environment.

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

::: {.story-card}

**Let the task choose the library**

The model can use a trusted package when the analysis calls for it.

:::

:::::

::::: {.right}

::: {.story-card}

**Manage the environment for the session**

Console retains requirements and prepares compatible package environments.

:::

:::::

::::::
::: {.takeaway}

Ordinary package use can request the dependency it needs.

:::

::: {.notes}

In my experience, models sometimes avoid installing a package because it sounds like a change to the user's global setup. They may settle for the libraries already available, even when another package would help.

Console resolves session requirements into a managed environment. The requirement configuration belongs to the session, while caches and prepared environments can be reused on disk. This gives the model access to CRAN and PyPI without installing into the user's global library.

Packages can still fail to install, and installation or build code runs outside the worker sandbox. The packages and preparation environment need to be trusted.

[Requirements and trust](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md)

:::
## Use the package; let the runtime prepare it {#r-resolution .deck-slide .story-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · packages

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R

:::

```python
console.send(r="library(data.table)")
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Python

:::

```python
console.send(python="import polars")
```

::::

:::::

::::::
::: {.sequence-strip}

Reach a missing package → resolve → activate → continue

:::

::: {.takeaway}

The live workspace stays available during supported additions.

:::

::: {.notes}

When execution reaches a supported missing-package operation, the runtime requests preparation, activates the result, and continues the original operation. The live workspace is preserved.

R preparation uses ir; managed Python uses uv. Resolution happens during execution, without pre-scanning the source or replaying the whole cell. Explicit requirements are available for version pins and distribution names that cannot be inferred from an import.

These calls are illustrative. Preparation needs a working resolver and the package's system prerequisites. Docker sessions use dependencies already installed in the image.

[Requirements and trust](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md)

:::

::: {.takeaway}

The server manages the session. The worker executes code inside the sandbox.

:::

::: {.notes}

The client talks to the Console server, which owns the session and its records. A relay carries code, input, controls, and results between the server and worker. The language runtimes execute inside the sandboxed worker.

Package resolvers are separate trusted processes outside the worker sandbox. A missing-package operation can request preparation; the resolver prepares the package, and the worker activates it and continues. Evaluated code keeps its own restricted permissions.

Installation and build code use the resolver's permissions. The appendix shows the private request and activation exchange in more detail.

[Implemented architecture](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [Sandbox configuration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Declare package requirements explicitly {#requirements .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · packages

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}

::: {.panel-label}

:::

```python
console.send(
  requirements={
    "r": ["dtplyr"],
    "python": ["scikit-learn==1.9.1"],
  },
)
```

::::
:::::
::::: {.right}

::: {.ownership-card}

Name a package without a version.

Pin a specific version when needed.

Prepare it before evaluating code.

:::

:::::
::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Requirements can also accompany a code cell in the same call.

:::

::: {.notes}

The model can declare requirements explicitly, either on their own or alongside a code cell. Preparation happens before the cell runs. This is useful for a version pin or a distribution name that cannot be inferred from an import.

This slide shows an illustrative request, not a captured successful preparation. The scikit-learn version comes from the Python reference capture. The older `data.table==1.17.8` rehearsal failed on the installed R toolchains and remains documented in the validation notes. Managed requirements are available only on targets that support preparation.

[Requirements and trust](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md)

## Use a Python library on the same data {#python .deck-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Use full runtimes · R and Python together

:::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

LLM client → Console · Python cell

:::

<!-- cells:python-ml -->
```python
console.send(python="""
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
import pandas as pd

frame = r.d
X = pd.get_dummies(frame[["temperature", "group"]])
model = RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, frame["response"],
                         cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
print(f"CV MAE: {-scores.mean():.3f}")
""")
```

::::


:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Captured Python result

:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("python-ml")
```

::::

::: {.notes}

Python reads the R data frame through `r.d` and uses scikit-learn's `RandomForestRegressor` and `cross_val_score`. The data stays in the session while the model switches to the library it needs.

The numerical result is a saved Console response. This example demonstrates access to both language ecosystems; it does not compare the statistical merits of the two models.

[runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md) · [requirements](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md)

:::
## Collect progress while the code keeps running {#wait-timeout .deck-slide .literal-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · waits and polls

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

LLM client → Console · running cell

:::

<!-- cells:progress -->
```python
console.send(r="""
  pb <- txtProgressBar(
    max = 20, style = 3, width = 20)
  for (i in 1:20) {
    Sys.sleep(0.15)
    setTxtProgressBar(pb, i)
  }
  close(pb)
""", timeout_ms=450)
```

::::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

LLM client → Console · collect new output

:::

<!-- cells:poll-next,poll-final -->
```python
console.send(timeout_ms=600)

console.send(timeout_ms=5000)
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Console → text · after 450 ms

:::

```{r}
#| label: progress-first
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("progress")
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Console → text · after 600 ms

:::

```{r}
#| label: poll-first
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("poll-next")
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Console → text · after 5000 ms

:::

```{r}
#| label: poll-last
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("poll-final")
```

::::

::: {.small-note}

The percentages depend on when each wait expires.

:::

:::::

::::::

::: {.takeaway}

The computation keeps running. An empty `send()` collects new output.

:::

::: {.notes}

`timeout_ms` controls how long a call waits for output. It does not stop the computation. Here, the first call waits 450 milliseconds and returns the progress collected so far while the same worker continues running.

An empty `send()` polls for more output without resubmitting the code. Each poll returns newly collected output. Carriage-return redraws within a response interval collapse to the current progress line; later polls can return another update.

The example uses R's `txtProgressBar`, with `Sys.sleep` standing in for work. These are literal captured responses, including the 600 ms and 5000 ms polls. Progress percentages depend on timing and are not guaranteed at a particular wait duration.

[send](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md) · [runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Protect the model’s context from oversized output {#bounded-output .deck-slide .literal-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · bounded output

:::


:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Call

:::

<!-- cells:flood -->
```python
console.send(r=r"""
  for (i in seq_len(10000)) {
    cat(sprintf("row %05d\n", i))
  }
  cat("fit complete\n")
""")
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

One tool response · shortened for display

:::

```text
row 00001
row 00002
row 00003

[output preview: middle omitted;
 raw output retained at
 .agents/console/sessions/<run>/
 outputs/call-000008.log]

row 09999
row 10000
fit complete
```

::::

:::::

::::::

::: {.notes}

Console bounds the text returned in a tool response so a large printout does not fill the model's context. It keeps the beginning and end, omits the middle, and gives the model a path to fuller retained output. A filesystem tool can inspect that file when needed.

The text budget is 8 KiB, with a separate image allowance. Raw retention is also bounded. The slide shortens the response for readability; `captures/flood.txt` contains the literal result.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Capture output below the language hooks {#retained-output .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · native output

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R · forked child writes through a pipe

:::

<!-- cells:r-fork-cat -->
```python
console.send(r=r"""
  job <- parallel::mcparallel({
    out <- pipe("cat", "w")
    cat("hello from fork\n", file = out)
    close(out)
  })
  invisible(parallel::mccollect(job))
""")
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Console response

:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("r-fork-cat")
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Python · write directly to stdout

:::

<!-- cells:python-fd -->
```python
console.send(python=r"""
import os
os.write(1, b"hello directly on fd 1\n")
""")
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Console response

:::

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("python-fd")
```

::::

:::::

::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Capture native output from the worker and its children.

:::

::: {.notes}

Console captures output below the language-level hooks. In the R example, a child process sends text through a pipe to the native `cat` command. Python writes directly to file descriptor 1, bypassing `sys.stdout`. Both results are captured.

The R example uses that specific route because plain `cat()` in a fork produced no visible text in the recorded build. The `23` after the Python output is the byte count returned by `os.write()`.

[Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Interrupt or restart the session {#session-controls .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · interrupt and restart

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Interrupt

:::

```python
console.send(control="interrupt")
```

::::

Interrupt a long-running computation. Keep the workspace.

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Restart

:::

```python
console.send(control="restart")
```

::::

Replace the worker. Start with fresh in-memory state.

:::::

::::::

Combine a control and a code cell in one call.

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R package development

:::

```python
# Run the package tests in a fresh session
console.send(control="restart", r="devtools::test()")

# Load the package, then evaluate more code
console.send(control="restart", r="devtools::load_all(); ...")
```

::::

::: {.takeaway}

Restart keeps prepared dependencies and starts the supplied cell in the new session.

:::

::: {.notes}

An interrupt asks the current computation to stop while keeping the workspace. It sends SIGINT, which code can catch or delay; changes already made remain. Restart replaces the worker with fresh in-memory state while retaining successfully prepared dependencies.

A control and a cell can share a call. For package development, a restart followed by `devtools::load_all()` or `devtools::test()` runs against the files on disk in a fresh R session. Launch these examples from the package directory. The calls are alternatives, and the ellipsis stands for further code.

A control-only interrupt can overlap a pending call. If an interrupt includes a new cell, that cell waits for the previous evaluation to stop. Restart discards R objects, Python state, the managed DuckDB catalog, debugger state, and unread input. The restart-and-test example was exercised with the saved control-operation fixture.

[Send operation contract](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md) · [Interruption and restart](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md#interruption)

:::
## Send input to an R prompt {#stdin .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · standard input

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Run code that asks for input

:::

<!-- cells:prompt -->
```python
console.send(r="""
  name <- readline("name> ")
  name
""")
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Response · waiting for input

:::

```{r}
#| label: stdin-prompt
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("prompt")
```

::::

:::::
::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Supply a line of standard input

:::

<!-- cells:prompt-answer -->
```python
console.send(stdin='Ada\n')
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Response · the same cell resumes

:::

```{r}
#| label: stdin-prompt-answer
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("prompt-answer")
```

::::

:::::
::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Send the answer through `stdin`, including the newline.

:::

::: {.notes}

`readline()` asks for a name and pauses the cell. Console returns the prompt and reports that the runtime is waiting for input.

The next call supplies `Ada` followed by a newline through `stdin`. The same cell resumes, assigns the answer to `name`, and prints it. The R code is not submitted again, and `stdin` does not add a newline automatically.

Both calls and responses come from the saved sandboxed session. Rendering reads those responses without opening an interactive prompt.

[Send operation contract](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md)

:::
## Send input to a paused debugger {#debugger .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · debugger

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Pause inside an R function

:::

<!-- cells:browser-start -->
```python
console.send(r="""
  inspect_mean <- function(x) {
    browser()
    mean(x)
  }

  inspect_mean(c(1, 2, 3))
""")
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Response

:::

```{r}
#| label: debugger-browser-start
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("browser-start")
```

::::

:::::
::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Inspect x

:::

<!-- cells:browser-x -->
```python
console.send(stdin='x\n')
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Response

:::

```{r}
#| label: debugger-browser-x
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("browser-x")
```

::::

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Continue

:::

<!-- cells:browser-continue -->
```python
console.send(stdin='c\n')
```

::::

:::: {.result-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Response

:::

```{r}
#| label: debugger-browser-continue
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("browser-continue")
```

::::

:::::
::::::

::: {.notes}

The `stdin` argument also supplies input to R's debugger. Here, `browser()` pauses execution inside a function. Sending `x` followed by a newline inspects the argument; sending `c` followed by a newline continues execution.

The session stays alive between calls while the model inspects values and decides how to continue. Each call is paired with its saved response from the same sandboxed session. Rendering does not enter the debugger, and `stdin` does not add newlines automatically.

[Send operation contract](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md)

## Run an interactive script in a fresh session {#restart-input .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · combined operations

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label .path-label}

./summarize.R

:::

```r
group <- readline("Group to summarize: ")
d <- readr::read_csv("./measurements.csv",
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
values <- d$response[d$group == group]
print(summary(values))
```

::::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Four arguments · one send call

:::

<!-- combined-cell:restart-script -->
```python
console.send(
  control="restart",
  requirements={"r": ["readr"]},
  stdin="A\n",
  r='source("./summarize.R")'
)
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

One response · captured from Console

:::

```{r}
#| label: restart-input-output
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
console_protocol("combined-input/restart-script")
```

::::

:::::

::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Prepare readr → restart → queue input → source the script.

:::

::: {.notes}

This call combines a restart, package requirements, input, and an R cell. Console prepares `readr`, replaces the worker, queues `A` and a newline, then sources the script. When `readline()` asks which group to summarize, the answer is already waiting. The worker-replacement notices and script output arrive in one response.

Run from `examples/` so the script and CSV are available. Preparation happens before the old worker is retired; a resolution failure at that stage leaves it available. Only the replacement receives the queued input. The script uses `readr::read_csv()` and prints its summary explicitly because `source()` does not automatically print visible expressions.

This request and response were captured together. Subsequent checks confirmed that old state was gone and group A was selected. If an answer depends on output not yet seen, supply it in a later input-only call.

[Send operation order](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md#operations)

:::
## The current send() interface {#full-signature .deck-slide .signature-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Drive a real session · the model-facing API today

:::

::: {.full-contract}

<pre class="signature-display">console.send(
  <span class="syntax-accent">r</span>=…, <span class="syntax-accent">python</span>=…, <span class="syntax-accent">sql</span>=…,    <span class="syntax-comment"># at most one language</span>
  control=…,               <span class="syntax-comment"># interrupt or restart</span>
  stdin=…,                 <span class="syntax-comment"># input for a read or prompt</span>
  requirements={r: …, python: …, duckdb: …},
  timeout_ms=…,            <span class="syntax-comment"># how long this call waits</span>
)</pre>

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Omit code to poll, supply input, control the session, or prepare dependencies.

:::

::: {.notes}

`send` accepts one language cell at a time: R, Python, or SQL. A call can also carry a control operation, standard input, package requirements, and a wait duration.

Code is optional. A call can poll, answer a prompt, interrupt or restart the session, or prepare dependencies. Explicit preparation and controls run before the evaluation wait. Code-free preparation cannot also carry nonempty `stdin`.

This is a schematic list of arguments, not a request to submit three language cells together. Requirements are exposed only when the target supports managed preparation.

[Send operation contract](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SEND_OPERATIONS.md) · [Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Choose between two built-in sandbox policies {#builtin-policies .deck-slide .literal-slide .policy-comparison}
::: {.kicker}

Enforce permissions · built-in policies

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

<h3>:read-only · default</h3>

- Read all host files your account can access.
- Write only in private temporary storage.
- Project files stay protected from writes.

:::: {.code-panel}

```bash
mcp-console serve \
  -c extends=:read-only
```

::::

:::::

::::: {.right}

<h3>:workspace</h3>

Adds writes in the **workspace**: the directory where you launch Console.

Write access stays denied for `.git`, `.agents`, `.codex`, and `.claude`. These subdirectories remain readable.

:::: {.code-panel}

```bash
mcp-console serve \
  -c extends=:workspace
```

::::

:::::

::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Both restrict networking, cover subprocesses, and clean up on restart. Deny sensitive paths explicitly.

:::

::: {.notes}

The default `:read-only` policy allows reads of host files available to the account and writes in private temporary storage. It restricts direct networking. Sensitive files need explicit read denials, and inherited environment variables may also need restrictions.

`:workspace` adds write access under the launch directory while protecting `.git`, `.agents`, `.codex`, and `.claude` from writes. Both policies cover the worker and its subprocesses. The leading colon is part of the preset name; `-c` overrides `extends` while retaining other project settings.

On restart and server shutdown, Console stops the worker and cleans up subprocesses and private storage, allowing a grace period before escalation. Linux waits for PID namespace retirement. macOS covers the owned process group and observed descendants, with an orphaning-race limitation. Runner death has no independent cleanup guarantee. Prepared dependencies, records, and project files persist.

`external-sandbox` and `unrestricted` are enforcement modes, not additional named presets.

[Sandbox configuration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md) · [Configuration layering](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/CONFIGURATION.md) · [Built-in runtime](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md)

:::
## Extend a built-in policy for the project {#private-inputs .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Enforce permissions · project configuration

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

::: {.ownership-card}

./data: read-only.

./secrets and ./.env: reads and writes denied.

Other workspace paths: writable, with protected project metadata.

:::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label .path-label}

.agents/console/config.yaml

:::

```yaml
extends: ":workspace"
sandbox:
  filesystem:
    entries:
      - path: {type: path, path: ./data}
        access: read
      - path: {type: path, path: ./secrets}
        access: deny
      - path: {type: path, path: ./.env}
        access: deny
```

::::

:::::

::::::
::: {.takeaway}

Set project permissions in .agents/console/config.yaml.

:::

::: {.notes}

Console reads `.agents/console/config.yaml` from the launch directory. This example extends `:workspace`, keeps the data directory read-only, and denies reads of the secrets directory and `.env`.

The paths should already exist. Native permission specificity is not determined by array order. Linux has documented limits on nested deny/read reopenings, so this example does not establish that arbitrary filesystem rules behave identically across platforms.

[sandbox](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Example: connect to a corporate data warehouse {#network-proxy .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Enforce permissions · network exceptions

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

::: {.ownership-card}

Route worker traffic through the managed proxy.

Allow the corporate warehouse host.

Use its HTTPS database API, or a SOCKS-aware database connection.

:::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label .path-label}

.agents/console/config.yaml · excerpt

:::

```yaml
sandbox:
  proxy:
    enabled: true
    domains:
      warehouse.example.com: allow
```

::::

:::::

::::::
::: {.takeaway}

The client still supplies its usual database credentials.

:::

::: {.notes}

A managed proxy can allow a specific HTTPS destination, such as a corporate data warehouse API, while retaining restrictions on other network access. The model still needs the usual credentials.

This slide shows a focused excerpt. The full configuration is in `examples/configs/network-proxy.yaml`, and the appendix lists the proxy fields. All seven scalar fields are required; `mode: full` still applies the destination rules.

Other database TCP protocols need a SOCKS-aware client or tunnel. Private-IP destinations need a literal-IP rule or local-network exception; allowing a hostname alone does not grant private-address access. The domains are placeholders and were not contacted.

[sandbox](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Example: develop a local Shiny app {#network-listener .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Enforce permissions · network exceptions

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

::: {.ownership-card}

allowLocalBinding: true

Run Shiny on the loopback interface.

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000` in your browser.

:::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label .path-label}

.agents/console/config.yaml · excerpt

:::

```yaml
sandbox:
  proxy:
    enabled: true
    allowLocalBinding: true
```

::::

:::::

::::::
::: {.takeaway}

`shiny::runApp("app", host = "127.0.0.1", port = 8000)`

:::

::: {.notes}

Allowing local binding lets the model start a Shiny app on a loopback port. The app can keep running while the model polls for output, then be interrupted when the work is finished.

This is a focused excerpt; `examples/configs/network-listener.yaml` contains the full configuration. The flag permits local networking beyond a single Shiny port. It does not provide a port-specific allowlist, a viewer, or automatic forwarding. Application behavior still needs to be checked on the chosen host.

[sandbox](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Run any command through the sandbox {#sandbox-command .deck-slide .story-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Enforce permissions · reuse the sandbox in your own application

:::

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

Public command-line interface

:::

```bash
mcp-console sandbox -- Rscript examples/sandbox-analysis.R
```

::::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.story-card}

**Choose the policy**

Use the same project config and command-line overrides.

:::
::: {.story-card}

**Run the command**

Console hands execution to the native sandbox runner. Its restrictions apply to the command and its children.

:::
::: {.story-card}

**Connect your application**

Use ordinary stdin, stdout, stderr, and exit status.

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}

Reuse the sandbox from your own tools and agent harnesses.

:::

::: {.notes}

The sandbox is also available as a command-line interface. An application can launch an ordinary command with standard input, output, error, and exit status, without starting an MCP server or persistent Console session.

The command after `--` runs under the project configuration and command-line overrides. Here, an R script reads the measurements CSV and prints model coefficients. Run it from the presentation directory. The native runner applies filesystem and network policy to the command and its subprocesses and owns their cleanup.

This path executes locally on macOS or Linux. It does not use the worker runtime, automatic package preparation, MCP output framing, or session transcripts. Target settings do not turn it into an SSH or Docker dispatcher. `external-sandbox` is a separate enforcement mode; advanced callers can supply a complete runner policy through `--config-env`. The native platform and lifecycle limits still apply.

[Sandbox integration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX.md) · [Sandbox configuration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Configure where the session runs {#execution-choice .deck-slide .story-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Where it runs · choose the execution host

:::

:::: {.three-col}

::: {.story-card}

**Local host**

Beside your project, using this machine’s files and compute.

:::

::: {.story-card}

**SSH host**

On an existing remote machine, beside its data and compute.

:::

::: {.story-card}

**Docker container**

Inside a prepared image, with the mounts you select.

:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}

Execution targets plug into the same session interface.

:::

::: {.notes}

Local execution is the default: the worker runs on the same host as the Console server. The user can instead configure an SSH host or a Docker container.

The session interface is separate from the execution environment. Local and SSH targets support managed package preparation. Docker uses preinstalled dependencies; adding uv and ir to an image does not enable preparation inside a running session.

[SSH execution](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SSH.md) · [Docker execution](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/DOCKER.md)

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Code runs beside the remote data. The client and session records stay local.

:::

::: {.notes}

With SSH, the client and Console server stay on the local machine while the relay and worker run on the remote host. Trusted package resolvers also run remotely, outside the worker sandbox.

This lets code run beside data already on that host. Results return over SSH, and the server keeps the session records locally. The remote worker and its subprocesses use the configured sandbox policy.

[SSH execution](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SSH.md)

## Point Console at the remote workspace {#ssh .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Where it runs · SSH

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

::: {.ownership-card}

Remote workspace and relative paths.

Remote runner and resolver.

Local MCP server and recordings.

:::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label .path-label}

.agents/console/config.yaml

:::

```yaml
extends: ":workspace"
target:
  transport:
    kind: ssh
    host: analysis-host
  workspace: /srv/projects/analysis
sandbox:
  filesystem:
    entries:
      - path: {type: path, path: ./data}
        access: read
```

::::

:::::

::::::


::: {.notes}

An SSH target names the host and the workspace where the worker starts. The workspace, data, and runtime prerequisites must already exist remotely. The client launches the local Console server as usual.

Here, the workspace policy and data-directory rule apply on the SSH host. `analysis-host` must be a configured OpenSSH destination, and `/srv/projects/analysis` must exist. Combining SSH and Docker targets is unsupported in this revision.

[ssh](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SSH.md) · [sandbox](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Run a prepared Docker image {#docker .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Where it runs · Docker

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}

Install Console, its runtimes, and analysis packages in the image.

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label .path-label}

From the mcp-console repository

:::

```sh
docker build \
  -f examples/docker/Dockerfile \
  -t my-console:analysis .
```

::::

:::::
::::: {.right}
:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label .path-label}

.agents/console/config.yaml

:::

```yaml
target:
  workspace: /workspace
  compute:
    kind: docker
    image: my-console:analysis
    pull: if_missing
    mounts:
      - source: .
        target: /workspace
        access: read_write
sandbox:
  filesystem: {kind: external-sandbox}
  network: enabled
```

::::
:::::
::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Docker sessions use preinstalled packages. Build the dependencies into the image.

:::

::: {.notes}

The Console repository includes a Dockerfile that builds the Linux executable and its native companion and installs R, Python, and analysis dependencies. Build the image from that repository, then configure its name and the project mount.

Docker sessions use preinstalled packages. Console does not resolve new dependencies inside the running container. This example delegates enforcement to Docker and uses bridge networking, without the destination restrictions from the proxy example.

The writable project bind includes metadata and recordings; `external-sandbox` adds no native `.git` or `.agents` write protection. The recipe and configuration were checked against revision `ea5c1e737f329a86d957b12d7d1f15690824e398` on October 2, 2026. No image build or container session was run for this presentation.

[Docker image recipe](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/ea5c1e737f329a86d957b12d7d1f15690824e398/examples/docker/Dockerfile) · [Docker execution](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/DOCKER.md)

send

```

Local host &nbsp; / &nbsp; SSH &nbsp; / &nbsp; Docker

:::



::: {.notes}

The model uses the same `send` interface whether the worker runs locally, over SSH, or in Docker. It submits cells, receives results, and uses the same input, wait, and control operations.

The user selects the execution host and its permissions. Available capabilities, including managed package preparation, depend on that target.

## Keep session logs and readable transcripts {#recording .deck-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

After the session · records

:::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Files under one session directory

:::

```text
.agents/console/sessions/<session-id>/
├── internal/
│   └── events.jsonl     # Calls, results, request metadata
├── outputs/
│   └── call-000003.log  # Raw cell output
├── artifacts/
│   └── *.png           # Captured plots
├── transcript.md       # Readable session history
└── transcript.qmd      # Executable code cells
```

::::
::: {.takeaway}

Full logs and a readable presentation of the session.

:::

::: {.notes}

Recording starts on the first `send` call. Each recorded session gets a directory under `.agents/console/sessions/`, relative to the Console server's working directory. For a remote worker, these files stay on the controller.

`internal/events.jsonl` records tool requests, assembled results, lifecycle metadata, and client-supplied metadata such as a thread ID. It is a structured journal, not a byte-for-byte wire capture or proof of delivery. The capture scripts retain the transport separately in `wire.jsonl`.

`outputs/` keeps fuller output when a response is shortened, with raw per-cell retention bounded at 1 GiB. `artifacts/` holds returned images. The server writes these files, so it can record a plot even when the worker has read-only project access. Other tools need access to that recording directory; it is not a general worker-writable export location.

Markdown presents the submitted calls and results in order. Quarto projects the submitted code into an editable document.

[Architecture](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)

:::

A reader can follow the session in order without replaying it.

## Turn the session into an editable starting point {#quarto-transcript .deck-slide .literal-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

After the session · records

:::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label .path-label}

report.qmd · edited copy of the session transcript

:::

```{r}
#| label: quarto-document
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| comment: ""
#| results: asis
header <- console_capture_text("excerpts/quarto-header")
header <- sub(
  "# Generated by MCP Console. Do not edit.\n",
  "",
  header,
  fixed = TRUE
)
header <- sub(
  "ir:\n",
  'ir:\n  exclude-newer: "2026-09-17"\n',
  header,
  fixed = TRUE
)
header <- sub("root.dir: [^\n]+", "root.dir: <project>", header)
header <- sub(
  "(?s)  packages:.*\n---",
  "  packages: [tidyverse, reticulate]\n---",
  header,
  perl = TRUE
)
cat(
  "````markdown\n",
  header,
  "\n",
  console_capture_text("excerpts/quarto-cell"),
  "\n````\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

::::

::: {.takeaway}

`ir render report.qmd` uses the recorded package snapshot date.

:::

::: {.notes}

The QMD transcript turns submitted R, Python, and SQL cells into executable chunks. It omits the recorded output, input, polls, and controls. The front matter records managed defaults and explicitly declared requirements in an `ir` section.

The example copies that source into `report.qmd`, shortens the package list, and adds a package cutoff date. With the data and connections available, `ir render report.qmd` can evaluate the edited analysis again.

The generated source needs curation: it can include failed or rejected calls, and its requirements are not a complete package inventory or environment lock. Rendering executes code outside the worker sandbox. SQL chunks need a configured DBI connection, and remote projections default to `eval: false` until an appropriate replay environment is supplied.

[ir Quarto integration](https://r-lib.github.io/ir/quarto.html) · [Architecture](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)

:::

## Possible extension: a session notebook {#future-notes .deck-slide .signature-slide .api-proposal}
::: {.kicker}

What’s next · API ideas, not implemented

:::

::: {.full-contract}

<pre class="signature-display">console.send(
  r=…, python=…, sql=…,    <span class="syntax-comment"># at most one language</span>

:::

::: {.small-note}

`note` is a working name; it could also be `comment`.

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Append intentions, observations, and conclusions alongside the code and results.

:::

::: {.notes}

Another possible extension is a `note` or `comment` argument. The model could record what it intends to check, then add observations or conclusions alongside the code and results, including notes without a code cell.

That would make the session record more useful as a lab notebook and provide prose for a later curated report. The name and behavior are still open; neither this argument nor the proposed session argument is implemented.

## Before an official release {#before-release .deck-slide .policy-slide}
::: {.kicker}

What’s next · platform status checked October 2, 2026

:::

- **Platforms:** macOS and Linux supported; Windows unsupported.
- **Python and SQL without R:** available.
- **Human-facing configuration:** readable YAML, discovery, and storage defaults.
- **Tool descriptions and evals:** convey capabilities clearly and use fewer tokens.
- **Curated session exports:** Quarto documents and timestamped lab notebooks.
- **Artifact handoff:** persistent output locations for other authorized tools.

::: {.takeaway}

The agent-facing API is largely complete. The human-facing experience needs another pass.

:::

::: {.notes}

As of October 2, 2026, macOS and Linux are supported, Windows is not, and Python and SQL can run without R. That status was checked at revision `ea5c1e737f329a86d957b12d7d1f15690824e398`.

The remaining items are design priorities. I'd like the configuration to be easier to read and write, with clearer discovery and storage defaults. Tool descriptions need to explain the available capabilities concisely, and evals can help check whether models find and use them.

Curated exports could let a model select parts of a session for a Quarto document. Artifact handoff also needs a design: an image or other output should persist where another authorized tool can retrieve it, without widening the worker's permissions.

These priorities come from the September 23 work list. They are not a release checklist or a commitment to particular APIs.

[Supported platforms](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/ea5c1e737f329a86d957b12d7d1f15690824e398/README.md) · [Python sessions without R](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/ea5c1e737f329a86d957b12d7d1f15690824e398/docs/BUILTIN_RUNTIME.md#python-sessions-without-r)

## Launch or install Console {#install-python .deck-slide .integration .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Get started · installation

:::

::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Recommended · launch an MCP server

:::


```bash
uv tool install mcp-console
```

```bash
uvx mcp-console
```

:::

::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Persistent Python installation · choose the integrations you need

:::

```bash
uv pip install "mcp-console[client,chatlas,openai,openai-agents,anthropic,codex]"
```

:::

::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R package · planned CRAN installation

:::

```r
install.packages("mcp.console")
```

:::

::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Register with Codex or Claude Code

:::

```bash
codex mcp add console -- uvx mcp-console serve
claude mcp add console -- uvx mcp-console serve
```

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Let `uvx` manage resolution and automatically pick up updates.

:::

::: {.notes}

`uvx mcp-console serve` resolves and launches the executable. Registry caching means it does not check for a new release on every launch; a version pin or compatible installed tool can retain an older version.

For a persistent installation in an existing Python environment, use `uv pip install`. The base package supplies the executable, and optional extras add the client integrations. Select the extras the application needs.

The R package is available from source with `pak::pak("github::t-kalinowski/mcp-console/r")`; CRAN installation is planned. The wrapper checks `PATH` unless a path or version is specified. When resolution is needed, it uses reticulate's uv integration to obtain the executable from PyPI rather than bundling it in the R package.

MCP clients register the server launch command and start it when needed. Client deadlines are separate from the wait duration supplied to Console.

[uv tools](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/tools/) · [Project README](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/README.md) · [Python clients and integrations](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/PYTHON.md) · [R package interface](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/r/README.md) · [Codex MCP](https://developers.openai.com/codex/mcp/) · [Claude Code MCP](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp)

## Connect Console to your agent harness {#interfaces .deck-slide .integration}
::: {.kicker}

Get started · clients

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}
:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

R · ellmer

:::

```r
library(ellmer)
library(mcp.console)

chat <- chat_openai()
chat$register_tool(console_tool())
chat$chat("Analyze measurements.csv with Console.")
```

::::
:::::
::::: {.right}
:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Python · chatlas

:::

```{.python code-line-numbers="2,5-6"}
from chatlas import ChatOpenAI
import mcp_console

chat = ChatOpenAI()
with mcp_console.MCPConsole() as console:
    chat.register_tool(mcp_console.chatlas.tool(console))
    chat.chat("Analyze measurements.csv with Console.")
```

::::
:::::
::::::

::: {.story-lead}

Also: OpenAI Responses and Agents SDK · Anthropic · Codex thread SDK · sync and async clients.

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Your chat and provider. A separate persistent Console worker.

:::

::: {.notes}

In ellmer, register `console_tool()` with the chat. In chatlas, register the adapter returned by `mcp_console.chatlas.tool(console)`. Other adapters cover the Anthropic SDK, OpenAI Responses, the Agents SDK, and the Codex thread SDK, alongside SDK-independent synchronous and asynchronous clients.

The application owns the conversation. Evaluated code runs in a separate persistent Console worker.

Adapter availability and image support depend on the installed release; the older wheel used for some captures lacks newer integrations. The chatlas registration example was checked with version 0.23.0 through a direct tool call, without a model API call. In that version, `register_tool()` reconstructs the schema from Python annotations. The seven arguments remain available; `set_tools()` preserves the server-provided schema when that is required.

## Example: use approved package repositories {#package-sources .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · package sources

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}

::: {.ownership-card}

Use a corporate mirror or a Posit Package Manager repository.

A curated repository exposes an approved set of packages and versions.

Restrict the resolver host's network access to enforce approved sources.

:::

:::::
::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label}

MCP client launch settings · YAML view

:::

```yaml
mcpServers:
  console:
    command: uvx
    args: [mcp-console, serve]
    env:
      PKG_CRAN_MIRROR: >-
        https://ppm.example.com/r/latest
      UV_DEFAULT_INDEX: >-
        https://ppm.example.com/python/simple
```

::::
:::::
::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Choose which packages are available for resolution.

:::

::: {.notes}

The resolvers can use a corporate mirror or Posit Package Manager repositories containing an approved set of packages. `PKG_CRAN_MIRROR` selects the R source used by ir's pak resolver; `UV_DEFAULT_INDEX` replaces uv's default Python index.

These settings belong in the Console server's launch environment, not `sandbox.environment`. For SSH, configure the remote preparation environment. The slide uses YAML for readability; clients that expect JSON need the equivalent JSON configuration.

Repository selection alone is not a package allowlist. Exclusive sourcing also depends on resolver-host network policy, additional repositories, explicit R remotes, bootstrap tools, preinstalled packages, and caches. The resolver runs outside the worker sandbox. A preinstalled environment is another option; Docker uses that approach, and an explicit `RETICULATE_PYTHON` selection disables managed Python additions.

The URLs are placeholders. Repository selection was checked with pak and uv, but no corporate PPM connection or end-to-end network restriction was tested.

[Resolver configuration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md#server-owned-uv-configuration) · [Worker environment scope](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md) · [pak configuration](https://pak.r-lib.org/reference/pak-config.html) · [uv package indexes](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/indexes/) · [PPM curated CRAN](https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/r-packaging/curated-cran.html) · [PPM curated PyPI](https://docs.posit.co/rspm/admin/python-packaging/curated-pypi.html)

## The complete proxy configuration {#proxy-options .deck-slide .config-slide .code-dense}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · network proxy

:::

:::::: {.two-col}
::::: {.left}

::: {.ownership-card}

Enable the proxy explicitly.

Set allowed destinations in `domains`.

Opt into local binding for Shiny.

Keep UDP, upstream proxies, and broad Unix-socket access off unless needed.

:::

::: {.small-note}

Empty rule maps grant no destinations. The default policy has no proxy.

:::

:::::
::::: {.right}
:::: {.code-panel}
::: {.panel-label .path-label}

.agents/console/config.yaml

:::

```yaml
extends: ":workspace"
sandbox:
  network: restricted
  proxy:
    enabled: true
    enableSocks5: true
    enableSocks5Udp: false
    allowUpstreamProxy: false
    dangerouslyAllowAllUnixSockets: false
    allowLocalBinding: false
    mode: full
    domains: {}
    unixSockets: {}
```

::::
:::::
::::::

::: {.notes}

This is the complete proxy object behind the warehouse and Shiny excerpts. Enabling it is explicit; it is not part of the default read-only policy.

The fields control destination rules, local binding, SOCKS, UDP, upstream proxies, and Unix sockets. The empty destination maps grant no destinations. `mode: full` permits the supported HTTP methods while retaining the destination policy.

All seven scalar fields are required when a proxy object is supplied. Console forwards them without filling in missing values. `domains` and `unixSockets` can be omitted, null, or empty. The shown values are an explicit baseline, not defaults applied automatically. The earlier excerpts omit surrounding fields; complete configurations are retained in `examples/configs/`.

[Sandbox configuration](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/SANDBOX_CONFIGURATION.md)

:::
## Follow a package-resolution request {#resolver-boundary .deck-slide .story-slide .literal-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Private worker protocol · illustrative paths

:::

:::::: {.two-col}

::::: {.left}

::: {.resolution-steps}

1. R reaches a missing package and the worker requests resolution.
2. The server prepares a library with `ir`, outside the worker sandbox.
3. The worker activates the library and continues the original load.

:::

:::::

::::: {.right}

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Worker → server

:::

```json
{"kind": "resolve_r",
 "packages": ["data.table"]}
```

::::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Server → worker

:::

```json
{"kind": "r_resolved",
 "library": "/cache/r/library"}
```

::::

:::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Worker → server

:::

```json
{"kind": "r_activated",
 "library": "/cache/r/library"}
```

::::

:::::

::::::

::: {.takeaway}

Trusted preparation can use the network while the worker remains restricted.

:::

::: {.notes}

The worker sends a package request through the relay to the server. The server validates it and asks a trusted resolver outside the sandbox to prepare the library. The worker adds the returned path to its live library search path and acknowledges activation before continuing the load. Only a matching activation from the current worker generation commits the retained environment.

These are private worker-protocol messages; the model does not send them as MCP tool calls. The field names follow the documented protocol, with `/cache/r/library` used as an illustrative path. Python uses the analogous `resolve_python` exchange to activate its prepared environment.

Installation and build code run with the preparation account's permissions. Caches can persist, and the worker keeps its own filesystem and network policy. On SSH, preparation happens on the remote host.

[Worker protocol](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/WORKER_PROTOCOL.md#nested-managed-r-resolution) · [Requirements and trust](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/REQUIREMENTS.md)

:::

## AGENTS.md gives the model project context {#development-agent-guidance .deck-slide .story-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · development practices · instructions in the repository

:::

::: {.development-intro}

A Markdown file of project instructions that a coding agent reads before making changes.

:::

:::: {.development-cards}
::: {.development-card}

**Where to look**

Architecture and module owners. Public interfaces. Development and validation commands.

:::
::: {.development-card}

**What to preserve**

Observable behavior. Readable errors and transcripts. Clear process and sandbox boundaries.

:::
::: {.development-card}

**How to change it**

A focused PR. A public regression test. Deterministic checks. Review of generated evidence.

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}

The instructions connect a requested change to the project’s contracts and checks.

:::

::: {.notes}

`AGENTS.md` gives a coding agent context about the repository: where to find the architecture and public contracts, which responsibilities belong to each process, and how to make and validate changes.

The instructions ask for coherent PRs, readable code, public-interface tests, and review of generated snapshots. Detailed behavior is specified by source, protocol documents, and tests. The instructions describe the intended process; checks and review provide evidence about a particular change.

[AGENTS.md at the analysis snapshot](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/657a5981983768967deed83c070973848ec800fb/AGENTS.md) · [Development guide](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/657a5981983768967deed83c070973848ec800fb/docs/DEVELOPMENT.md)

## The development loop starts with behavior {#development-loop .deck-slide .story-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · development practices · the prescribed workflow

:::

:::: {.development-steps}
::: {.development-step}

**1 · Describe**

Choose one observable behavior and the public interface that exercises it.

:::
::: {.development-step}

**2 · Reproduce**

Add a public test and see it fail before changing the implementation.

:::
::: {.development-step}

**3 · Implement**

Make the change, rerun the test, and inspect any updated transcripts.

:::
::: {.development-step}

**4 · Validate**

Format and run the full checks. Require CI and review on the current PR revision.

:::
::::

::: {.takeaway}

The test suite gives the agent and the reviewer a shared description of expected behavior.

:::

::: {.notes}

For a behavior change, the project instructions call for a failing public regression or acceptance test before implementation. A focused rerun and snapshot review follow the change, then formatting and the full check suite. Passing CI and approval from the configured reviewer are required on the current revision before merging.

For an internal refactor, existing public tests provide the contract. Tests use observable checkpoints rather than timing guesses, and generated transcripts preserve behavior while normalizing incidental details.

This describes the written workflow at the snapshot date, not an audit of every historical PR.

[Working rules in AGENTS.md](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/657a5981983768967deed83c070973848ec800fb/AGENTS.md) · [Validation ladder](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/657a5981983768967deed83c070973848ec800fb/docs/DEVELOPMENT.md)

:::

::::: {.two-col}

:::: {.left}

::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Checked-in YAML · request

:::

```yaml
send:
  r: |
    cores <- parallel::detectCores()
    stopifnot(
      length(cores) == 1L,
      !is.na(cores),
      cores >= 1L
    )
    writeLines("R core detection available")
```

:::

::::

:::: {.right}

::: {.result-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

:::

        R core detection available
  isError: false
```

Readable code, arguments, output, and errors. Not escaped JSON strings.

Source excerpt: `detects_cpu_cores.yaml` · initialization document omitted.

The production wire protocols use JSON, while the reviewable test transcripts use YAML. This saved snapshot shows R code checking CPU detection and printing a stable message. A reviewer can read the request and result without escaped JSON strings or a machine-specific expected core count.

## Synchronize; do not sleep and hope {#test-determinism .deck-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · Development practices

:::

::: {.big-statement}

Start → checkpoint → release → assert

:::

::: {.takeaway}

Explicit gates for output, cancellation, restart, and cleanup.

:::

::: {.notes}

Concurrency and liveness tests use gates and checkpoints to establish that the relevant state has been reached. A sleep alone cannot show that output was drained, an interrupt delivered, or a resource retired.

The sequence illustrates that testing approach. Individual fixtures need synchronization tied to the behavior they observe.

## Portable behavior; real capability checks {#test-capabilities .deck-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · Development practices

:::

::::: {.two-col}

:::: {.left}

::: {.big-statement}

Shared cases<br>direct + sandboxed

:::

::::

:::: {.right}

::: {.big-statement}

Capability fixtures<br>SSH · Docker · SBX

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.takeaway}

Fake peers establish protocol contracts; real targets establish target behavior.

:::

::: {.notes}

Portable cases can run across execution modes, with capability discovery determining which fixtures apply. A skipped fixture provides no validation of that target.

Deterministic peers test orchestration, while real containers and microVMs are needed to test their cleanup behavior. Lifecycle and security assertions cover properties that textual snapshots alone cannot establish.

## Snapshots are generated evidence {#snapshot-review .deck-slide}
::: {.kicker}

Appendix · Development practices

:::

::: {.code-panel}

::: {.panel-label}

Run, regenerate, review

:::

```bash
scripts/test --update BOUNDARY/SUITE::CASE

git diff -- tests/snapshots/
```

:::



::: {.notes}

Transcripts are generated by running tests, then reviewed as diffs. Expected output is not hand-edited to make a test pass. Readable YAML helps reviewers inspect changed behavior; separate assertions cover facts a transcript cannot show.

`BOUNDARY/SUITE::CASE` in the command is a placeholder for an actual test selector.

::::: {.two-col}

:::: {.left}

::: {.takeaway}

Packaging, launch, schemas, images, shutdown, and cleanup are part of the contract.

:::

::: {.notes}

The installed product includes the executable, native companions, Python interfaces, the R wrapper, and their launch and shutdown behavior. Running a development binary alone does not establish that the installed bundle or every adapter works.

Release evidence should include packaging and integration checks, with real-target validation reported separately. This slide describes the scope to check, rather than claiming every proposed integration test already exists.

[Boundary test guide](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/tests/boundaries/README.md) · [Release and installed bundle](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/RELEASE.md) · [Python clients and integrations](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/docs/PYTHON.md) · [R package interface](https://github.com/t-kalinowski/mcp-console/blob/main/r/README.md)

:::
